sections.markdown:
## C — Safe driving rules: speed limits, passing and lane markings, keeping right, yielding, pedestrians in crosswalks, intersections, highway entry and exit, and turning regulations
Knowledge domain: the core rules of the road a New Jersey driver must know — statutory speed limits and driving to conditions, when and where passing is allowed, keeping to the right, who must yield, the full stop owed to pedestrians in crosswalks, controlled and uncontrolled intersections and traffic circles, entering and leaving highways, and how to position the vehicle for right and left turns.

FACT_ID: sec06-F01 | anchor: A01
Going 10 mph or more over the 65 mph limit doubles the fine, and most other moving violations in a 65 mph zone carry doubled fines too. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec06-F02 | anchor: A01
Speeding raises both the chance of a crash and how severe it is, and it leaves the driver less time to react to hazards or correct mistakes. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec06-F03 | anchor: A01
Unless another limit is posted, the New Jersey speed limit is 25 mph in school zones and in business or residential districts. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec06-F04 | anchor: A01
Unless another limit is posted, the limit in suburban business and residential districts is 35 mph. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec06-F05 | anchor: A01
Unless another limit is posted, the limit on rural roads without posted limits is 50 mph. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec06-F06 | anchor: A01
The 55 mph limit applies to certain state highways, as posted, and to interstates. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec06-F07 | anchor: A01
The 65 mph limit applies only to certain interstate highways where it is posted. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec06-F08 | anchor: A02
Never drive faster than the weather, road or traffic allows, whatever the posted limit says; driving too fast for conditions can bring a moving violation. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec06-F09 | anchor: A02
Always slow down on narrow or winding roads, at intersections and railroad crossings, on hills, at sharp or blind curves, near pedestrians or hazards, on wet or icy roads and when visibility is limited. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec06-F10 | anchor: A02
When the road surface and traffic are normal, New Jersey law forbids holding up traffic by driving too slowly. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec06-F11 | anchor: A03
When both center lines are solid, no passing is allowed. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec06-F12 | anchor: A03
When one center line is broken, passing is allowed only from the side with the broken line. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec06-F13 | anchor: A03
When both center lines are broken, passing is allowed from either side. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec06-F14 | anchor: A03
Every pass must be finished before the center lines turn solid again. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec06-F15 | anchor: A03
The Safe Corridors law, signed in July 2003, doubles fines on designated state highways for offenses such as speeding and aggressive driving. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec06-F16 | anchor: A04
Passing is normally done on the left; passing on the right is permitted only where the road has more than one lane in your direction and traffic is moving in two or more steady lines, or where the driver ahead is turning left and there is room. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0067]

FACT_ID: sec06-F17 | anchor: A04
Passing on the right shoulder of the road is never allowed and is against the law. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0067]

FACT_ID: sec06-F18 | anchor: A04
Do not pass on a hill or curve or whenever you cannot see far enough ahead, at an intersection or railroad crossing, on narrow bridges or in underpasses or tunnels, where signs or center lines forbid it, or behind a vehicle stopped to let a pedestrian cross. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0067]

FACT_ID: sec06-F19 | anchor: A04
New Jersey law requires driving on the right half of the road, as close as practical to the right edge or curb, except when passing or on a one-way street. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0067]

FACT_ID: sec06-F20 | anchor: A04
On a multi-lane road, use the available lane nearest the right edge or curb, except when overtaking another vehicle or preparing for a left turn. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0067]

FACT_ID: sec06-F21 | anchor: A04
Always yield to police cars, fire engines and ambulances that are using sirens or flashing lights, and to a train approaching a railroad crossing. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0067]

FACT_ID: sec06-F22 | anchor: A05
A driver must come to a full stop, not merely slow or yield, for a pedestrian in a marked crosswalk or one crossing at an unmarked crosswalk at an intersection. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0068]

FACT_ID: sec06-F23 | anchor: A05
Stay stopped until the pedestrian has cleared both your lane and the next lane going in your direction. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0068]

FACT_ID: sec06-F24 | anchor: A05
Stop for every pedestrian still in a crosswalk even if the signal has changed to Don't Walk. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0068]

FACT_ID: sec06-F25 | anchor: A05
Never overtake a vehicle that has stopped at a crosswalk for a pedestrian, and never block or park in a crosswalk. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0068]

FACT_ID: sec06-F26 | anchor: A05
Not stopping for a pedestrian can cost a fine of up to $500, a jail term of up to 25 days, community service, a suspension of driving privileges of up to six months, and two motor vehicle points. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0068]

FACT_ID: sec06-F27 | anchor: A06
Most crashes happen at intersections, and a single solid white line across the road there means stopping behind it for a traffic signal or sign. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec06-F28 | anchor: A06
At a multi-way stop, a driver who arrives at the same moment as another yields to the one on the right, and also yields to any vehicle already stopped there. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec06-F29 | anchor: A06
At a yield sign, slow down and give the right-of-way to traffic on the crossing road, stopping if needed. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec06-F30 | anchor: A06
When turning left, yield to oncoming traffic and stop for pedestrians in the crosswalk. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec06-F31 | anchor: A06
At a stop sign, come to a complete stop within five feet of the nearest crosswalk or stop line, then enter only after yielding to pedestrians and to any traffic close enough to be an immediate hazard. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec06-F32 | anchor: A07
Approaching an uncontrolled crossroad, slow down and be ready to stop for traffic from either side, and when coming out of a private road or driveway yield to all traffic on the main road. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec06-F33 | anchor: A07
As a general rule at an uncontrolled intersection, the vehicle on the left yields to the vehicle on the right. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec06-F34 | anchor: A07
A traffic signal that is dark because of a power failure or other malfunction is treated as a 4-way stop. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec06-F35 | anchor: A07
New Jersey has no set rules for traffic circles: the circle's established flow pattern usually decides the right-of-way, a major highway running through it usually dominates, and stop or yield signs at the entrances also govern. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec06-F36 | anchor: A07
Highways, parkways and turnpikes are divided roads with speeds up to 65 mph and no direct intersections, entered by an acceleration lane, and drivers must yield to traffic already on the main road. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec06-F37 | anchor: A08
When entering a highway, speed up to the flow of traffic as you leave the acceleration lane and avoid stopping completely in that lane. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec06-F38 | anchor: A08
If you miss an exit, continue to the next one, and never back up on an exit ramp or deceleration lane. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec06-F39 | anchor: A09
In a weave lane, which serves as both an entrance and an exit, the driver coming from the entrance ramp must yield to the driver leaving the expressway. [A09]
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec06-F40 | anchor: A10
If your vehicle breaks down, pull as far onto the shoulder or median as you can, turn on the flashers, raise the hood, stay inside with the seat belt on and doors locked, and never get into a stranger's vehicle. [A10]
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec06-F41 | anchor: A11
Unless a No Turn on Red sign is posted, a right turn on red is allowed after a full stop, and the driver must yield to all oncoming traffic and pedestrians first. [A11]
Source: [A11 -> pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec06-F42 | anchor: A11
For a right turn, approach as far to the right as possible, close to the curb or parked cars, and do not swing wide or into another lane. [A11]
Source: [A11 -> pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec06-F43 | anchor: A12
When two vehicles facing each other both turn left, each should turn to the left of the center of the intersection when it is safe. [A12]
Source: [A12 -> pdf-0075]

FACT_ID: sec06-F44 | anchor: A12
For a left turn from a one-way road onto another one-way road, approach in the left lane and turn into the left lane of the new road. [A12]
Source: [A12 -> pdf-0075]

FACT_ID: sec06-F45 | anchor: A12
For a left turn from a two-way road onto a four-lane highway, turn into the lane nearest the center line, which is the passing lane, and move right out of it when traffic allows. [A12]
Source: [A12 -> pdf-0075]

Misconceptions: a posted limit is not a safe speed in bad conditions; a yield or slowdown is not enough for a pedestrian in a crosswalk, the law demands a full stop; the right shoulder is never a passing lane; a dark traffic signal is not a free pass, it becomes an all-way stop; in a weave lane the entering driver, not the exiting one, yields.
Mnemonics: twenty-five for school, business and homes, thirty-five for the suburbs, fifty for open country, fifty-five for state highways and interstates, sixty-five only where posted; the left yields to the right; broken line on your side means you may pass.
Glossary: acceleration lane means the extra lane at a highway entrance used to reach traffic speed; deceleration lane means the extra lane at an exit used to slow down; weave lane means a single lane used both to enter and to leave an expressway; Safe Corridors means designated state highways where fines are doubled; uncontrolled intersection means one with no signal or regulatory sign.
Dynamic facts: the list of Safe Corridor highways changes as the Commissioner of Transportation designates or removes them, and fines and penalties can change; confirm them on the New Jersey Department of Transportation and MVC websites.
